newsitem.title: CUBA: Hurricane Lili hits Cuban mainland, avoids capital.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Lili hits Cuban mainland, avoids capital.

text.p: Hurricane Lili hit Cuba's mainland early on Friday but was unlikely to bring its full force to bear on the island's capital after it killed at least 10 people when it lashed Central America.

To the relief of Havana's two million residents, the hurricane set a more easterly course than anticipated and appeared set to cross Cuba and head north into the Florida Straits without causing major damage in the capital.

Lili pounded central Cuba with sustained 90 mph (145 kph) winds and torrential rains as the Bahamas braced for the coming storm, Miami's National Hurricane Centre said. A hurricane watch was in effect for the central Bahamas and a tropical storm warning remained in effect for the Florida Keys from Key Largo to the Dry Tortugas including Florida Bay.

Cuban forecaster Jose Rubiera told state television that at 6 a.m. local time (1100 GMT) the storm was over the Cienaga de Zapata, a low-lying marshy area in the western province of Matanzas. It was heading north-northeast and was expected to take about three to four hours to cross Cuba, Rubiera said.

Areas to the east of the hurricane's course were the most affected, with heavy rain falling in the provinces of Matanzas, Cienfuegos, Sancti Spiritus and Ciego de Avila. Reports from the Isle of Youth said there had been damage to crops such as bananas but there was no word of casualties.

Sugar cane may also be affected by the hurricane. The cane, a crucial hard currency earner for Cuba, is within two or three months of being harvested. With the hurricane on a more easterly course, the large cane-growing areas of central Cuba were likely to be whipped by strong winds and heavy rain.

Strong winds gusted from the early hours of Friday turning Havana into a wind-blown ghost town. Some streets were littered with tree branches and several electricity poles fell during the night. The state electricity company cut power to most parts of the capital before dawn to minimise damage to power lines during the passage of the hurricane.

President Fidel Castro, following the hurricane closely, travelled early on Friday to Batabano on the southern coast in Havana province. On Thursday night, he welcomed a group of people evacuated from their homes in Havana to make-shift dormitories set up in the Council of State, his office in Revolution Square. Earlier, he urged citizens to heed warnings to evacuate their homes if they were viewed as vulnerable.

Havana Communist Party First Secretary Esteban Lazo said the rate of evacuations from homes in a poor state of repair had improved. Earlier, people seemed not to take the warning seriously, worrying they might be robbed in their absence.

State radio said that by Friday morning about 75,000 people had been evacuated from vulnerable buildings. The evacuated also included some foreign tourists taken from hotels on the seafront to other lodging.
Havana international airport was closed late on Thursday until further notice and the national airline Cubana cancelled domestic and foreign flights for Friday.
So far the highest death toll was in Nicaragua, where Civil Defence officials said five people had drowned in swollen rivers across the country over the past four days and 200 were left homeless.
In Costa Rica four people were killed in river tragedies and in Honduras a toddler died when his house was washed away in a shantytown on the edge of the capital Tegucigalpa.
